conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Started up to and including day 5, the POP gives immediate protection. Started at any other time (here day 8), 48 hours of additional contraception are needed for the cervical mucus to thicken sufficiently.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the progestogen-only pill is prescribed a 5-day course of amoxicillin for a chest infection. What is the correct advice about her contraception?
options: No additional precautions are needed — ordinary antibiotics do not reduce POP efficacy
Use condoms during and for 7 days after the antibiotics
Switch to the copper IUD for the duration
Take a double dose of the POP while on antibiotics
Stop the POP until the antibiotics finish
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: No additional precautions are needed — ordinary antibiotics do not reduce POP efficacy
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Non-enzyme-inducing (ordinary) antibiotics such as amoxicillin do NOT reduce the efficacy of the POP — a common misconception. No extra precautions are needed. Only enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin) reduce efficacy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman with epilepsy taking carbamazepine wants the progestogen-only pill. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Switch her to the combined pill, which is unaffected by enzyme inducers
The POP is fully effective with carbamazepine, so no change is needed
Double the POP dose to compensate for the increased metabolism
Carbamazepine reduces POP efficacy; switch to a method unaffected by enzyme inducers
Ordinary antibiotics are the only drug interaction worth worrying about
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Carbamazepine reduces POP efficacy; switch to a method unaffected by enzyme inducers
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Carbamazepine is an enzyme-inducing anticonvulsant that reduces the efficacy of the POP (and of the COCP, patch, ring and implant), making the POP UKMEC 3. The right move is a method unaffected by enzyme inducers — the copper IUD, the intrauterine system or the injection. The IUS and injection are hormonal but unaffected.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A 29-year-old woman started on the traditional POP 4 months ago reports ongoing unpredictable spotting. She is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: Reassure, but as it has persisted beyond 3 months, exclude pregnancy, STI and cervical pathology
Prescribe long-term tranexamic acid to suppress the unpredictable spotting
Add oestrogen tablets alongside the POP to bring the bleeding under control
Stop the POP immediately, since ongoing bleeding means the method has failed
Switch straight to the copper IUD without any further assessment or tests
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Reassure, but as it has persisted beyond 3 months, exclude pregnancy, STI and cervical pathology
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Irregular vaginal bleeding is the most common POP side effect and the leading reason for discontinuation. It often settles, but because it has persisted beyond 3 months, other causes (pregnancy, STI, cervical/endometrial pathology) should be excluded before attributing it to the pill and considering a switch.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: Which statement about the mechanism of the traditional progestogen-only pill is correct?
options: Its main action is preventing implantation of a fertilised egg
It works by delivering a low dose of oestrogen locally to the cervix
It reliably inhibits ovulation in every cycle, as the combined pill does
It suppresses FSH and LH as effectively as the combined pill does
It works mainly by thickening cervical mucus; ovulation is inhibited in only about 50–60% of cycles
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: It works mainly by thickening cervical mucus; ovulation is inhibited in only about 50–60% of cycles
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The traditional POP works mainly by thickening cervical mucus (with endometrial thinning and reduced tubal motility); it inhibits ovulation in only ~50–60% of cycles. This short-lived mucus effect is why timing is strict (3-hour window). Desogestrel/drospirenone POPs additionally inhibit ovulation reliably.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman with current breast cancer requests the progestogen-only pill. What is the correct advice?
options: She can use the POP at half the usual daily dose
Current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for the POP — offer a non-hormonal method
The POP is safe here, as it contains no oestrogen at all
Only the combined pill is contraindicated, not the POP
She can use it provided the cancer is hormone-receptor negative
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for the POP — offer a non-hormonal method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Current breast cancer is the main UKMEC 4 (absolute) contraindication to the POP, because it is hormone-sensitive. A non-hormonal method (e.g. copper IUD) should be offered. Past breast cancer is UKMEC 3.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the traditional POP becomes pregnant and presents with lower abdominal pain. What is the key clinical concern?
options: She should simply stop the POP and be reviewed again in a month
The POP causes miscarriage, so no further action is needed now
A higher proportion of POP pregnancies are ectopic, so an ectopic must be excluded
The pregnancy is certainly intrauterine, so no imaging is required
Pain at this stage always reflects normal implantation cramping
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: A higher proportion of POP pregnancies are ectopic, so an ectopic must be excluded
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Because the traditional POP does not always suppress ovulation, a slightly higher proportion of pregnancies that occur are ectopic. A POP user who becomes pregnant with abdominal pain must have an ectopic excluded, even though any contraception lowers the absolute ectopic risk compared with using none.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman wishes to switch from the COCP to the POP without a gap in protection. What is the correct advice?
options: Take the usual 7-day break from the combined pill, then start the POP
Start the POP during the pill-free week, which gives immediate cover
She always needs 7 days of extra cover whenever she switches method
Start the POP straight after the last active COCP pill, with no hormone-free interval
She cannot switch directly and must use condoms for a full month
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Start the POP straight after the last active COCP pill, with no hormone-free interval
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Starting the POP directly after the last active pill of a correctly used combined pack, with no hormone-free interval, gives immediate protection. Not every combined pack is 21 active pills, so the rule is about the last active pill rather than 'day 21'. Starting during or after a pill-free interval would need additional cover.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A breastfeeding woman 10 days postpartum wants a reliable oral contraceptive. What is the most appropriate advice about the POP?
options: The POP is UKMEC 1 in breastfeeding and can be started now
The POP significantly reduces milk supply and should be avoided
She should use the combined pill instead while she is breastfeeding
The POP is contraindicated while she is breastfeeding
She must wait until 6 weeks postpartum, as with the combined pill
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: The POP is UKMEC 1 in breastfeeding and can be started now
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The POP is UKMEC 1 in breastfeeding and can be started immediately postpartum; only a small amount of progestogen enters breast milk and it is harmless to the infant. Started up to and including day 21 postpartum it is effective immediately; after day 21, 2 days of additional contraception are needed. Combined methods, by contrast, are UKMEC 4 while breastfeeding under 6 weeks postpartum.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the traditional POP vomits 90 minutes after taking her pill. What is the correct advice?
options: Take two extra pills now to be sure of the dose
Nothing further is needed, as the pill was almost certainly absorbed
Take a replacement pill as soon as possible and continue the pack
Stop the POP for the rest of the pack and use condoms
Switch to the combined pill, which is less affected by vomiting
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Take a replacement pill as soon as possible and continue the pack
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Vomiting within 2 hours of taking the POP means absorption may be incomplete, so she should take a replacement pill as soon as possible and continue the pack. If that replacement is taken within her normal window (3 hours for a traditional POP, 12 hours for desogestrel) no extra precautions are needed; if not, follow the missed-pill advice and use condoms until 48 hours of correct pill-taking.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: Which progestogen-only pill has the longest missed-pill window and what is that window?
options: Drospirenone POP — 24 hours
Desogestrel POP — 12 hours
Levonorgestrel POP — 3 hours
Norethisterone POP — 6 hours
All POPs share a 3-hour window
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The drospirenone POP has the longest window at 24 hours (and a 4-day inactive-tablet interval, with condoms for 7 days rather than 48 hours after a missed tablet). Desogestrel is 12 hours and the traditional POPs (levonorgestrel, norethisterone) are 3 hours.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A 32-year-old woman with migraine with aura wants oral contraception. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: No oral contraception is safe in a woman with migraine with aura
Migraine with aura contraindicates the POP as well as the combined pill
The combined pill is UKMEC 4 (stroke risk); the POP has no oestrogen and is suitable
The combined pill is fine at a low dose in migraine with aura
She should use the combined patch instead, as it avoids first-pass
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: The combined pill is UKMEC 4 (stroke risk); the POP has no oestrogen and is suitable
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined (oestrogen-containing) methods because of ischaemic stroke risk. The POP contains no oestrogen and is a suitable oral alternative, being usable in almost everyone including this group.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the traditional progestogen-only pill misses two consecutive pills. What is the correct action regarding the missed pills?
options: Stop the pill and wait for her next period before restarting the pack
Take three pills at once to catch up on the missed doses
Take just one pill (the most recent), continue the pack at the usual time, and use condoms for 48 hours
Discard the pack and start a new one from the first tablet the same day
Take both missed pills together, then carry on with the rest of the pack as usual
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Take just one pill (the most recent), continue the pack at the usual time, and use condoms for 48 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: If more than one POP is missed, she takes only one pill (the most recent) as soon as she remembers, continues the pack at the usual time, uses condoms until pills have been taken correctly for 48 hours, and considers emergency contraception if she had unprotected sex during the unprotected window.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: Which of the following best explains why the POP has 'far broader eligibility' than the COCP?
options: It protects against sexually transmitted infections as well as pregnancy
It requires no daily adherence, unlike the combined pill
It is more effective than the combined pill in every cycle
It contains no oestrogen, so it avoids the oestrogen-related VTE and arterial risks
It has a longer missed-pill window than any other contraceptive method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: It contains no oestrogen, so it avoids the oestrogen-related VTE and arterial risks
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The POP's broad eligibility comes from having no oestrogen: it avoids the VTE and arterial-disease risks that drive the COCP's UKMEC 3/4 contraindications (migraine with aura, VTE history, age 35 or over plus smoking, hypertension, breastfeeding under 6 weeks postpartum). Its trade-offs are stricter timing and less predictable bleeding, and current breast cancer remains a contraindication.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A 34-year-old woman with heavy, painful periods wants long-acting reversible contraception that will also help her bleeding. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (52 mg)
Combined oral contraceptive pill
Copper intrauterine device
Contraceptive implant
Progestogen-only injectable
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The LNG-IUS thins the endometrium, making periods lighter (often amenorrhoea) and is first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding — so it treats both her contraceptive need and her menorrhagia. The copper IUD would worsen her bleeding. The implant and the injection are long-acting but are not treatments for heavy menstrual bleeding.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman wants a hormone-free, long-acting method and does not mind heavier periods. She has no gynaecological pathology. Which is most appropriate?
options: Copper intrauterine device
Combined contraceptive patch
Contraceptive implant
Progestogen-only pill
Levonorgestrel IUS
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The copper IUD is the non-hormonal LARC of choice for a woman who wants to avoid hormones and accepts that periods may become heavier, longer and more painful. It is >99% effective and unaffected by weight or enzyme inducers.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: Which statement about the mechanism of the copper IUD is correct?
options: Copper ions are toxic to sperm and ova and it impairs implantation
It thins the endometrium via local progestogen
It works mainly by suppressing ovulation
It thickens cervical mucus as its principal action
It acts by raising systemic progesterone levels
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Copper ions are toxic to sperm and ova and it impairs implantation
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The copper IUD is non-hormonal: copper ions are toxic to sperm (reducing motility and survival) and ova, preventing fertilisation, and it produces an endometrial inflammatory reaction that impairs implantation. It does not suppress ovulation or involve hormones.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman has a 52 mg levonorgestrel IUS fitted purely for contraception. Using the current UK licence, how long can it remain in place before replacement?
options: 5 years
3 years
10 years
It never needs changing
8 years
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The 52 mg levonorgestrel IUS is licensed for 8 years for contraception, extended from 5. The heavy menstrual bleeding licence (5 years) and the HRT endometrial-protection licence (4 years, with (FSRH) supporting 5) were not extended.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A 46-year-old woman has a 52 mg LNG-IUS inserted for contraception. Until what age can it be relied upon for contraception?
options: It must be changed at 8 years even though she is 45 or over
Until age 55
Until age 60
Until it is 5 years old, then remove regardless of age
Until age 50
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: A 52 mg levonorgestrel IUS inserted at age 45 or over can be used for contraception until age 55, when contraception can generally stop — a useful shortcut for women aged 45 or over. A copper IUD inserted at age 40 or over can stay until the menopause. If the IUS is also being used as the HRT progestogen it must still be changed at the HRT licence interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman has a copper IUD inserted on day 18 of her cycle. When is she protected against pregnancy?
options: After 48 hours
Only from her next period
After 7 days
After 14 days
Immediately
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The copper IUD is effective immediately after insertion at any point in the cycle — which is also why it is the most effective emergency contraceptive. The '7-day' rule (unless inserted days 1–5) applies to the hormonal IUS, not the copper IUD.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman has an LNG-IUS inserted on day 15 of her cycle. What advice about additional contraception should she be given?
options: Use additional contraception for 5 days
None — it works immediately
Use additional contraception for 7 days
Use additional contraception until her next period
Use additional contraception for 48 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The IUS is reliable after 7 days, so 7 days of extra cover are needed unless it was inserted in the first 5 days of the cycle (when it is immediate). Inserted on day 15, she needs 7 days of additional contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: Three weeks after an IUS insertion, a woman develops pelvic pain, fever and purulent discharge. What is the most important consideration about the timing of PID risk relative to insertion?
options: The device must always be removed immediately in any pelvic infection
PID risk is highest 6 months after insertion
PID risk from the device persists lifelong
Insertion-related PID risk is confined to about the first 20 days; screen for STIs before fitting
PID risk is only increased with the copper, not the hormonal, device
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Insertion-related PID risk is confined to about the first 20 days; screen for STIs before fitting
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The small increase in PID risk attributable to insertion is confined to roughly the first 20 days, after which risk returns to baseline — which is why STI screening beforehand is important. She should be assessed and treated for PID; the device can often be left in situ if she responds to antibiotics, but removal is considered if no improvement in 48–72 hours.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman with an IUD in situ has a positive pregnancy test. What is the key clinical priority?
options: Reassure her that pregnancy with a coil is impossible
Immediately start folic acid and do nothing else
Arrange an urgent termination of pregnancy
Remove the coil only once she is past 12 weeks
Exclude an ectopic — a higher proportion of such pregnancies are ectopic
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Exclude an ectopic — a higher proportion of such pregnancies are ectopic
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: If pregnancy occurs with an IUD/IUS in situ, a higher proportion are ectopic (even though the absolute ectopic risk is lower than with no contraception, because overall pregnancy is rare). An ectopic must be actively excluded with a scan. If intrauterine and threads are visible, early removal is generally advised to reduce miscarriage/infection risk.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman returns unable to feel her IUS threads. She had unprotected sex last week. What is the correct sequence of management?
options: Immediately book a hysteroscopy without any imaging
Insert a second device straight away
Exclude pregnancy, advise extra contraception, and locate the device (ultrasound)
Reassure and review in 6 months
Prescribe antibiotics and discharge
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Exclude pregnancy, advise extra contraception, and locate the device (ultrasound)
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: Lost threads may indicate expulsion, perforation or pregnancy. First exclude pregnancy and advise additional contraception, then locate the device with ultrasound (and abdominal X-ray if not seen in the uterus, to detect perforation). Management depends on where the device is found.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: Which of the following is a contraindication specific to the levonorgestrel IUS but not the copper IUD?
options: Current breast cancer
Distorted uterine cavity
Wilson's disease
Current pelvic inflammatory disease
Copper allergy
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: Current breast cancer is a contraindication to the hormonal IUS (it contains progestogen). Wilson's disease and copper allergy are specific to the copper IUD. Current PID and cavity distortion are contraindications common to both.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman with Wilson's disease requests long-acting intrauterine contraception. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: She must use the combined pill instead
Neither intrauterine method can ever be used
Both intrauterine devices are contraindicated in Wilson's disease
A copper IUD is ideal for her
The copper IUD is contraindicated; the levonorgestrel IUS is a suitable alternative
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: The copper IUD is contraindicated; the levonorgestrel IUS is a suitable alternative
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: Copper is contraindicated in Wilson's disease (and copper allergy), so the copper IUD should be avoided. The hormonal LNG-IUS contains no copper and is a suitable intrauterine alternative for her.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: Which statement about the effect of body weight and enzyme-inducing drugs on intrauterine contraception is correct?
options: Efficacy is reduced in women with a high BMI
Weight over 90 kg halves the efficacy of the IUS
Both the copper IUD and IUS remain fully effective regardless of weight or enzyme inducers
Only the copper IUD is affected by enzyme inducers
Enzyme inducers reduce efficacy, so the dose must be doubled
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Both the copper IUD and IUS remain fully effective regardless of weight or enzyme inducers
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: A key advantage of intrauterine methods is that efficacy is unaffected by body weight/BMI or enzyme-inducing drugs (the copper acts locally and the IUS releases progestogen directly into the uterus). This contrasts with the patch (≥90 kg), LNG emergency pill (weight), and oral/implant methods affected by enzyme inducers.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman had an LNG-IUS fitted 2 months ago and complains of frequent irregular spotting. She is otherwise well with normal examination. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Reassure — irregular spotting is common in the first 3–6 months and settles
Start tranexamic acid indefinitely to control the spotting
Switch her to a copper IUD which causes less bleeding
This indicates infection and needs a course of antibiotics
Remove the device immediately, as it has clearly failed
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Reassure — irregular spotting is common in the first 3–6 months and settles
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: Irregular bleeding and spotting are common in the first 3–6 months after IUS insertion and typically settle, often to very light or absent periods (amenorrhoea) with less dysmenorrhoea. Reassurance is appropriate once pathology/infection/malposition is excluded on history and examination.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman needs emergency contraception after UPSI on day 12 of her cycle and would like ongoing contraception too. She asks which intrauterine device can serve both purposes. What is correct?
options: Both devices work equally well as emergency contraception
Neither intrauterine device works as emergency contraception
The IUS can be used as emergency contraception and left for ongoing use
Only the IUS works as emergency contraception
The copper IUD is effective as emergency contraception and can be left in for ongoing contraception
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: The copper IUD is effective as emergency contraception and can be left in for ongoing contraception
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive: it can be fitted up to 5 days after unprotected sex, or up to 5 days after the earliest expected ovulation, whichever is later — and can be left in for ongoing long-term contraception. It works mainly by copper being toxic to sperm and ova, with inhibition of implantation as a back-up. The levonorgestrel IUS is not recommended as emergency contraception in the UK.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: Which factor increases the risk of uterine perforation during IUD/IUS insertion?
options: A high BMI
A previous normal vaginal delivery years ago
Insertion during menstruation
Insertion in a breastfeeding woman in the early postpartum period
Use of the copper rather than hormonal device
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Insertion in a breastfeeding woman in the early postpartum period
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: Perforation is rare (~1–2/1000) but the risk is higher with a fixed/retroverted uterus and in the early postpartum period (particularly while breastfeeding) — one reason IUD/IUS insertion is avoided in the 48-hour to 4-week postpartum window. The device type and BMI do not materially change perforation risk.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A perimenopausal woman with hypertension and heavy periods needs contraception. Combined methods are unsuitable because of her blood pressure. Which option best addresses all her issues?
options: Contraceptive patch
Combined oral contraceptive pill
Copper IUD
Levonorgestrel IUS
Vaginal ring
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: The LNG-IUS is ideal: it provides highly effective contraception, treats her heavy menstrual bleeding (first-line), avoids oestrogen (safe in hypertension), and can later serve as the progestogen arm of HRT. The copper IUD would worsen her bleeding, and oestrogen-containing methods are unsuitable given her hypertension.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.question: A woman is counselled before copper IUD insertion. Which statement about its reversibility and duration is correct?
options: It causes permanent sterilisation of the uterus
Rapid return of fertility after removal; copper devices last 5 or 10 years by copper content
Fertility only returns after two normal menstrual cycles
All copper IUDs last exactly 3 years, whatever the type
Fertility takes up to a year to return after removal
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.answer: Rapid return of fertility after removal; copper devices last 5 or 10 years by copper content
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.explanation: Intrauterine contraception is fully reversible with a rapid return of fertility after removal. Copper devices with 380 mm2 or more of copper (stem and arms) are licensed for 10 years; those with less copper (stem only) for 5 years. If she is not switching straight to another method, she should use condoms or avoid sex for 7 days before removal.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A 25-year-old woman attends 3 days after unprotected sex on day 13 of a regular 28-day cycle. She wants the most effective option and is happy to have a device fitted. What is the best emergency contraception?
options: Reassurance — it is too late for any method
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally
Levonorgestrel 3 mg orally
Copper intrauterine device
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: The copper IUD is the most effective EC (~99%), works at any point in the cycle (post-fertilisation effect), and is unaffected by weight or enzyme inducers. It should be offered first to all eligible women and, being within 5 days of UPSI, is appropriate and gives ongoing contraception. Oral methods are less effective.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman weighing 82 kg (BMI 29) requests emergency contraception 24 hours after UPSI. She declines an IUD and wants an oral method. If levonorgestrel is chosen, what is the correct dose?
options: 1.5 mg repeated after 12 hours
1.5 mg — standard dose
3 mg — but only if she is also taking an enzyme-inducing drug
3 mg — the dose should be doubled as her weight is >70 kg / BMI >26
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: 3 mg — the dose should be doubled as her weight is >70 kg / BMI >26
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Levonorgestrel efficacy falls with higher body weight, so the dose is doubled to 3 mg if BMI >26 or weight >70 kg. She meets both thresholds. (Ulipristal or, ideally, a copper IUD would also be reasonable given her BMI.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A 30-year-old woman had UPSI 100 hours (just over 4 days) ago. She declines a copper IUD. Which oral emergency contraceptive is appropriate?
options: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg — still within window
No oral method is effective beyond 72 hours
A repeat course of the combined pill
Levonorgestrel 3 mg
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg — licensed up to 120 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg — licensed up to 120 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Levonorgestrel is only licensed up to 72 hours. At 100 hours the appropriate oral option is ulipristal acetate, which is effective up to 120 hours (5 days). The copper IUD (up to 5 days after UPSI, or 5 days after earliest ovulation) would be the most effective if she reconsiders.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman takes ulipristal acetate for emergency contraception and wants to start the combined pill to continue regular contraception. What is the correct advice?
options: She can never use hormonal contraception after ulipristal
Start the pill immediately but double the first dose
Wait 5 days after ulipristal before starting the pill, using barrier methods meanwhile
Start the combined pill immediately with no extra precautions
Take levonorgestrel as well to cover the gap
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Wait 5 days after ulipristal before starting the pill, using barrier methods meanwhile
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Ulipristal and progestogens interfere with each other, so hormonal contraception should be delayed until 5 days after UPA, with barrier methods used in the interim. (After levonorgestrel, by contrast, hormonal contraception can be quick-started immediately.) UPA and LNG must not be combined in the same episode.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A 22-year-old woman took levonorgestrel 1.5 mg for emergency contraception and vomited 90 minutes later. What is the correct advice?
options: Switch to ulipristal now
Insert a copper IUD only
Repeat the levonorgestrel dose, as vomiting occurred within 3 hours
Nothing further is needed as the dose was absorbed
Wait to see if her period comes
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Repeat the levonorgestrel dose, as vomiting occurred within 3 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: If vomiting occurs within 3 hours of taking either oral emergency contraceptive, the dose should be repeated (or a copper IUD offered), because absorption may have been incomplete.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A breastfeeding mother requests emergency contraception with ulipristal acetate 30 hours after UPSI. What is the current (FSRH) advice regarding breastfeeding?
options: Express and discard breast milk for 1 week after the dose
She must switch entirely to formula feeding
Breastfeeding must stop for 24 hours only
Ulipristal is absolutely contraindicated in breastfeeding
No interruption of breastfeeding is needed after a single ulipristal dose
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: No interruption of breastfeeding is needed after a single ulipristal dose
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Current advice (FSRH) is that no interruption of breastfeeding is needed after a single ulipristal dose — transfer into breast milk is negligible, and the older 'express and discard for a week' advice has been superseded. Levonorgestrel has no breastfeeding restriction either. Some product literature still advises avoiding breastfeeding for a week, so patients may see conflicting information.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman whose severe asthma remains poorly controlled despite oral corticosteroids requests emergency contraception. Which oral method warrants particular caution?
options: Neither oral method has any interaction with asthma at all
Both oral methods are equally contraindicated in asthma
Ulipristal — not recommended in severe asthma poorly controlled on steroids
The copper IUD is contraindicated in asthma
Levonorgestrel — because of its progestogen content and dose
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Ulipristal — not recommended in severe asthma poorly controlled on steroids
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Ulipristal is a selective progesterone receptor modulator with anti-glucocorticoid activity, so it is not recommended in severe asthma that is insufficiently controlled by oral corticosteroids. Levonorgestrel or a copper IUD would be preferable here.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman on carbamazepine (an enzyme-inducing drug) requests emergency contraception after UPSI. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Ulipristal is the preferred oral option as it is unaffected by enzyme inducers
Offer a copper IUD (unaffected by enzyme inducers); if oral, use levonorgestrel 3 mg — ulipristal is not recommended
Double the ulipristal dose to 60 mg
No method works while on enzyme inducers
Standard-dose levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is fully effective
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Offer a copper IUD (unaffected by enzyme inducers); if oral, use levonorgestrel 3 mg — ulipristal is not recommended
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: The copper IUD is unaffected by enzyme inducers and is preferred. If oral EC is used, levonorgestrel should be doubled to 3 mg (enzyme inducers lower its levels); ulipristal is not recommended with enzyme inducers (its efficacy may be reduced and dose-doubling is not established).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: Which statement about the mechanism of oral emergency contraception is correct?
options: It is equally effective at every point in the menstrual cycle
It reliably terminates an established pregnancy
It works mainly by delaying/inhibiting ovulation, so is ineffective once ovulation has already occurred
It works by making the uterus toxic to sperm
Levonorgestrel primarily prevents implantation of a fertilised egg
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: It works mainly by delaying/inhibiting ovulation, so is ineffective once ovulation has already occurred
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Oral EC (both LNG and UPA) works mainly by delaying or inhibiting ovulation, so it is ineffective once ovulation has occurred and does not disrupt an established pregnancy. This is precisely why the copper IUD — which also blocks implantation — is more effective and works at any point in the cycle.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman had UPSI 6 days ago on day 10 of a regular 28-day cycle. Her earliest likely ovulation is around day 14. She is now on day 16. Is any emergency contraception still appropriate?
options: No — it is beyond all windows
Only ulipristal, as it works up to 6 days
A copper IUD can still be inserted, as it is within 5 days of the earliest likely ovulation
Reassure her that pregnancy is impossible
Levonorgestrel is appropriate as it works up to 7 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: A copper IUD can still be inserted, as it is within 5 days of the earliest likely ovulation
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: The copper IUD can be inserted within 5 days of UPSI OR up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation. With earliest ovulation ~day 14, day 16 is within 5 days of that, so a copper IUD is still appropriate — a key advantage over oral EC, which is beyond its window and would be ineffective if ovulation has occurred.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman took ulipristal 2 days ago and now realises she had further UPSI last night. She wants emergency contraception again. What is the correct advice?
options: She can take ulipristal again, but should not take levonorgestrel in this episode
She should wait until her next period before any further EC
Only a copper IUD is permitted for her now
She must take levonorgestrel this time, to avoid an overdose
She cannot use any emergency contraception again in the same cycle
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: She can take ulipristal again, but should not take levonorgestrel in this episode
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Ulipristal can be used more than once in a cycle, so a repeat dose is appropriate for the new episode. However, UPA and LNG should not be combined in the same episode (they interfere), so she should not switch to levonorgestrel now. A copper IUD remains the most effective option if acceptable.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A 15-year-old requests emergency contraception. Besides providing EC, what are the essential additional considerations?
options: No additional considerations — just provide the pill
Refuse treatment until she is 16
STI risk assessment and safeguarding, applying Fraser guidelines for under-16s
Mandatory parental consent before any treatment
Automatic referral to the police
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: STI risk assessment and safeguarding, applying Fraser guidelines for under-16s
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: EC provision should always include STI risk assessment and safeguarding. For an under-16, the Fraser criteria are assessed and documented; parental consent is not mandatory if she meets them. A child under 13 can never legally consent to sexual activity (Sexual Offences Act 2003), so any such disclosure requires a safeguarding referral whatever her apparent competence. In 13–15s explore the partner's age, coercion and exploitation — but do not withhold emergency contraception while doing so.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman is prescribed levonorgestrel for EC and wants to start the progestogen-only pill straight away. What is the correct advice about quick-starting?
options: She should take a second dose of levonorgestrel first
Hormonal contraception is contraindicated after EC
She cannot start any hormonal method for a week
She must wait 5 days as with ulipristal
She can start the POP immediately after levonorgestrel, with condoms or abstinence for 2 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: She can start the POP immediately after levonorgestrel, with condoms or abstinence for 2 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Unlike ulipristal (which requires a 5-day wait), regular hormonal contraception can be quick-started immediately after levonorgestrel. For the POP additional cover is needed for 2 days; for the combined pill, patch, ring, implant or injection it is 7 days. A pregnancy test should follow no sooner than 21 days after the last UPSI.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: Which of the following is the single most important advantage of the copper IUD over oral emergency contraception, aside from its higher efficacy?
options: It also protects against sexually transmitted infections
It works only in the first 24 hours
It can be left in situ to provide ongoing long-term contraception
It is more effective the later in the cycle it is inserted
It is cheaper than oral EC
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: It can be left in situ to provide ongoing long-term contraception
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Beyond being the most effective EC and unaffected by weight/enzyme inducers, a major bonus of the copper IUD is that it can remain in place as ongoing long-term contraception — turning an emergency into a durable solution. It does not protect against STIs.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman's period is 8 days late two weeks after taking levonorgestrel emergency contraception. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait another month before testing
Reassure her — EC always prevents pregnancy
Give a repeat dose of levonorgestrel
Insert a copper IUD now
Perform a pregnancy test, as the period is more than 5–7 days late
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Perform a pregnancy test, as the period is more than 5–7 days late
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: A pregnancy test is advised if the next period is more than 5–7 days late or lighter than usual after EC, because oral EC is not 100% effective (and is ineffective if ovulation had already occurred). Her period is 8 days late, so testing is indicated. A test is also advised routinely no sooner than 21 days after the last UPSI, because a quick-started hormonal method may prevent a recognisable period.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman with BMI 34 requests oral emergency contraception 12 hours after UPSI and firmly declines a copper IUD. Which oral option is preferable and what caveat applies?
options: Neither oral method works, so nothing can be offered to her
Ulipristal acetate — less weight-sensitive, though efficacy still falls above BMI 30
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg — body weight does not affect it at all
Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg — a lower dose suits higher BMI
Ulipristal is contraindicated in obesity and must be avoided
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Ulipristal acetate — less weight-sensitive, though efficacy still falls above BMI 30
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: At high BMI, oral EC is less reliable; the copper IUD is best (unaffected by weight) but she declines it. Of the oral options, ulipristal is less weight-sensitive than levonorgestrel, though its efficacy is still reduced above BMI 30 — so she should be counselled about this and advised to test if her period is late.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: Which statement correctly summarises the time windows for the three methods of emergency contraception?
options: Levonorgestrel up to 120 hours, ulipristal up to 72 hours, copper IUD up to 3 days
Copper IUD up to 3 days, both oral methods up to 24 hours
All three work up to 5 days after UPSI
All three must be used within 24 hours
Copper IUD up to 5 days, ulipristal up to 120 hours, levonorgestrel up to 72 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Copper IUD up to 5 days, ulipristal up to 120 hours, levonorgestrel up to 72 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Copper IUD: within 120 hours (5 days) of the first UPSI in the cycle, or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation, whichever is later. Ulipristal: up to 120 hours (5 days). Levonorgestrel: up to 72 hours (3 days), with efficacy falling as time passes.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.question: A woman took a progestogen-only pill this morning (her regular method) but had a missed-pill risk and now wants emergency contraception. Why might ulipristal be a poor choice here, and what is preferred?
options: She should stop her POP for a month before taking any EC
No emergency contraception is needed while she is on the POP
Levonorgestrel cannot be used alongside the POP at all
Ulipristal is preferred here because it is the stronger of the two
Recent progestogen blunts ulipristal, and it delays hormonal contraception by 5 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.answer: Recent progestogen blunts ulipristal, and it delays hormonal contraception by 5 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.explanation: Progestogen taken in the 7 days before ulipristal can reduce UPA's efficacy, and hormonal contraception must be delayed 5 days after UPA — awkward when she wants to keep taking her POP. A copper IUD (most effective, unaffected) or levonorgestrel (allows immediate resumption of the POP) is usually the more practical choice.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A 24-year-old woman wants a combined hormonal method but struggles to remember a daily pill and has frequent bouts of Crohn's-related diarrhoea. She has no contraindications to oestrogen. Which method is most suitable and why?
options: Copper IUD — no hormones to absorb
Combined oral contraceptive pill — best cycle control
Combined contraceptive patch — weekly, and absorption is unaffected by diarrhoea
Progestogen-only injection — given only every 13 weeks
Progestogen-only pill — must be taken within a strict window
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Combined contraceptive patch — weekly, and absorption is unaffected by diarrhoea
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: The patch is a combined method changed only weekly (easier adherence than a daily pill) and, being transdermal, its absorption is unaffected by vomiting or diarrhoea — a specific advantage over the COCP in someone with malabsorptive/GI illness. The POP needs precise daily timing; DMPA/IUD are not combined methods if she specifically wants CHC benefits.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman using the combined contraceptive patch forgot to change her Week 2 patch and realises it has been left on for 3 days longer than it should have been (72 hours late). What is the correct advice?
options: Apply a new patch, start a new 4-week cycle, use barrier cover for 7 days ± EC
Apply a new patch immediately; no extra precautions are needed
Take the progestogen-only pill instead for the next week
Continue with the same patch until the usual change day
Stop the patch and wait until her next period to restart
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Apply a new patch, start a new 4-week cycle, use barrier cover for 7 days ± EC
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: A mid-cycle delay of 48 hours or more means the patch may not be working. She should apply a new patch, treat that as day 1 of a new 4-week cycle, use 7 days of barrier cover, and consider emergency contraception if she had unprotected sex in the preceding 5 days (or during an extended patch-free interval). A delay of under 48 h would have needed no extra cover.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman on the patch forgets to remove her Week 3 patch and takes it off 1 day into what should have been her patch-free week. What is the correct advice?
options: Skip the next patch entirely and use condoms for a month
She needs emergency contraception straight away
Remove it now and apply the next patch on the usual cycle start day
Continue the over-run patch for another full week
Start a new cycle immediately with 7 days extra cover
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Remove it now and apply the next patch on the usual cycle start day
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: An over-run at the end of Week 3 is low-risk because the hormone-free interval is not extended — the excess hormone simply shortens the patch-free week. Remove the patch as soon as possible and apply the next patch on the usual cycle start day (even if bleeding). No extra contraception is required.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman finishes her patch-free week but forgets to apply the first patch of her new cycle until 3 days late. What is the correct advice?
options: Apply two patches at once to make up the missed hormone
No action is needed — the first patch of a cycle is not time-critical
Apply the patch now, use additional contraception for 7 days, and consider EC
She is fully protected as long as she had a withdrawal bleed
Wait until the next scheduled change day before restarting the patch
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Apply the patch now, use additional contraception for 7 days, and consider EC
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: A late start to a new cycle extends the hormone-free interval — the highest-risk error because ovulation may occur. She should apply the patch now, use 7 days of additional contraception, and consider emergency contraception if she had unprotected sex during the extended patch-free interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A 30-year-old woman weighing 96 kg requests the contraceptive patch. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Weight has no effect on any hormonal contraceptive
The patch is the ideal method at her weight
She must lose weight before any contraception can be prescribed
She should use two patches at once to compensate
Patch efficacy may be reduced at ≥90 kg — consider an alternative method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Patch efficacy may be reduced at ≥90 kg — consider an alternative method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Patch efficacy may be reduced at body weights of 90 kg or more, so an alternative method should be considered. Doubling up on patches is not recommended. This is a patch-specific weight caveat, separate from BMI, where BMI 35 or over is UKMEC 3 for all combined methods.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A 37-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes a day asks for the contraceptive patch. What is the correct advice?
options: The patch is fine because it is transdermal rather than oral
Only the combined pill, not the patch, is contraindicated by smoking
The patch carries no VTE risk, unlike the combined pill
Age 35 or over with 15 or more cigarettes a day is UKMEC 4 for the patch — offer a non-oestrogen method
She can use the patch if she halves the number of cigarettes
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Age 35 or over with 15 or more cigarettes a day is UKMEC 4 for the patch — offer a non-oestrogen method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: The patch is a combined (oestrogen-containing) method with the same UKMEC categories and oestrogen risks as the COCP. At 37 smoking 20 a day she is UKMEC 4, so an oestrogen-free method (progestogen-only pill, implant, IUS, copper IUD or the injection) should be offered. Cutting down to fewer than 15 a day would make her UKMEC 3, not UKMEC 1 — the risks would still usually outweigh the benefits.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman's combined contraceptive patch has partially peeled off during week 2 and she is unsure how long ago it detached. What is the correct advice?
options: Reapply it and take a combined pill for the rest of the week
Treat it as 48 h or more: new patch, new cycle, 7 days extra cover ± EC
Wait until the next change day and apply a fresh patch then
Stick it back down with medical tape and keep the same change day
No action is needed, as some of the patch is still attached
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Treat it as 48 h or more: new patch, new cycle, 7 days extra cover ± EC
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: If detachment duration is unknown it is managed as ≥48 hours: apply a new patch, start a new cycle, use 7 days of additional cover, and consider EC if relevant. If a patch will not re-stick you apply a new one — you must never use tape to hold a patch on.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman starts the contraceptive patch on day 8 of her menstrual cycle. What advice about immediate efficacy should she be given?
options: She needs 48 hours of extra cover only
Because she started after day 5, she needs 7 days of additional (barrier) cover
She should wait until her next period to start
It is effective immediately regardless of cycle day
No extra cover is needed but she must avoid sex for 24 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Because she started after day 5, she needs 7 days of additional (barrier) cover
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Started up to and including day 5 the patch is immediately effective. Started at any other time (here day 8) it requires 7 days of additional barrier cover while ovulation suppression establishes — exactly as for the COCP, and pregnancy should be reasonably excluded first.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: What is the primary mechanism by which the combined contraceptive patch prevents pregnancy?
options: Inhibition of ovulation via suppression of FSH and LH
Blocking implantation only
A local spermicidal effect on the skin
Creating a hostile endometrium as the sole mechanism
Thickening cervical mucus as its main action
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Inhibition of ovulation via suppression of FSH and LH
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Like the COCP, the patch's primary action is inhibition of ovulation through oestrogen/progestogen suppression of FSH and LH. Thickened cervical mucus and a thinned endometrium are secondary contributory mechanisms.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman using the patch develops new migraine with aura. What is the correct advice regarding her contraception?
options: Add a daily low-dose aspirin and continue the patch
Continue the patch — migraine is not relevant to transdermal methods
Reduce her to a patch-free fortnight instead of stopping
Switch her to the combined pill, which is safer in migraine
Stop the patch — migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined methods
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Stop the patch — migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined methods
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for all combined hormonal methods (increased ischaemic stroke risk), including the patch. It should be stopped and she should switch to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method. Switching to the COCP would carry the identical contraindication.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: Which statement about the contraceptive patch regimen is correct?
options: It is changed daily like a nicotine patch
One patch lasts for the whole 4-week cycle
It is worn continuously and is never removed at all
The patch-free week comes before the three active weeks
A new patch weekly for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: A new patch weekly for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: The standard regimen is a new patch each week for 3 weeks (same change day), then a patch-free fourth week producing a withdrawal bleed, before starting the next cycle. Extended/tailored regimens omitting the patch-free week are also possible.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman on the patch asks whether it protects her against chlamydia and other STIs. What is the correct advice?
options: STI protection is only lost if the patch detaches
Only against bacterial, not viral, STIs
Yes, the oestrogen provides some STI protection
No — the patch offers no STI protection; condoms are still needed
Yes, because it thickens cervical mucus
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: No — the patch offers no STI protection; condoms are still needed
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Like all hormonal methods, the patch offers no protection against sexually transmitted infections. Condoms are still required for STI protection alongside it.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A woman using the combined contraceptive patch develops a red, itchy rash at each application site. What is a reasonable option, and what is a key non-contraceptive point in her favour compared with the COCP?
options: She should cover the patch with a plaster to stop the rash
Skin irritation is a recognised drawback; a benefit is that patch absorption is unaffected by vomiting/diarrhoea
Skin irritation means she has a serious oestrogen allergy and must stop all contraception
Skin irritation is unique to the COCP not the patch
The rash indicates the patch is not working
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Skin irritation is a recognised drawback; a benefit is that patch absorption is unaffected by vomiting/diarrhoea
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Skin/application-site irritation is a recognised disadvantage of the patch (rotating sites can help; if intolerable, switch method). A distinct advantage the patch retains over the COCP is that, being transdermal, its absorption is unaffected by vomiting or diarrhoea.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: A 26-year-old woman with a personal history of a provoked DVT 2 years ago wants the contraceptive patch because she dislikes daily pills. What is the correct advice?
options: Transdermal oestrogen carries no VTE risk at all
The patch is safe here because it avoids first-pass metabolism
She can use the patch provided she also takes an anticoagulant
The patch is fine as long as she takes it for less than a year
A personal history of VTE is UKMEC 4 for the patch — offer a non-oestrogen method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: A personal history of VTE is UKMEC 4 for the patch — offer a non-oestrogen method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: The patch is a combined oestrogen-containing method and carries the same VTE risk and UKMEC contraindications as the COCP. A personal history of VTE is UKMEC 4, so an oestrogen-free method (POP, implant, IUS, copper IUD, DMPA) should be offered instead — the transdermal route does not remove the oestrogen-related thrombotic risk.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 47-year-old non-smoker with no cardiovascular risk factors and a BMI of 24 attends for contraceptive review. She is still having regular periods and wishes to continue a combined pill for her heavy, painful periods and hot flushes. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: She should switch to the progestogen-only injectable as the safest option at her age
She can continue a combined pill (≤30 micrograms ethinylestradiol) up to age 50, then switch to a safer method
She no longer needs contraception as she is perimenopausal
She must stop combined hormonal contraception immediately because she is over 40
Combined contraception is absolutely contraindicated over 45
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: She can continue a combined pill (≤30 micrograms ethinylestradiol) up to age 50, then switch to a safer method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Age ≥40 alone is only UKMEC 2 for CHC. In a low-risk woman (non-smoker, no CVD/VTE risk factors) a lower-dose pill (≤30 micrograms ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel/norethisterone) can be continued to age 50, and gives useful perimenopausal benefits (bleeding control, vasomotor symptoms, bone density). At 50 she switches to a progestogen-only/non-hormonal method. She is not menopausal and still needs contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 52-year-old woman has had a copper IUD in situ for 3 years (inserted at age 49). She has had no periods for 14 months. She asks when the device can be removed and contraception stopped. What is the correct advice?
options: Check an FSH level before removing the copper IUD
She can stop after 1 year of amenorrhoea, so the device can be removed now
She needs 2 years of amenorrhoea before stopping
Remove now — she is over 50 so no longer fertile
She must keep it until age 55 regardless of bleeding
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: She can stop after 1 year of amenorrhoea, so the device can be removed now
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: For a non-hormonal method, contraception can stop after 1 year of amenorrhoea if aged ≥50 (or 2 years if <50). She is 52 with 14 months of amenorrhoea, so the copper IUD can be removed now. (Everyone can also simply stop at 55 regardless of bleeding.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 43-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding wants effective contraception that also treats her periods, and asks about future HRT. Which single option best meets all three needs?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill
Copper intrauterine device
Progestogen-only pill
52 mg LNG-IUS
Progestogen-only injectable
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: 52 mg LNG-IUS
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: The 52 mg LNG-IUS provides contraception, is first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding, and can serve as the progestogen arm of HRT — a uniquely three-in-one solution for the perimenopausal woman. The copper IUD does not help bleeding; the injectable causes a small loss of bone mineral density and raises cardiovascular concerns over 40, so it is not the best fit here.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 51-year-old woman who is amenorrhoeic on a progestogen-only pill asks whether she can stop contraception. A single FSH level is 42 IU/L. What is the correct advice?
options: She can stop contraception 1 year after this FSH result
Repeat FSH in 6 weeks off all hormones before deciding
FSH cannot be interpreted on the POP so the test is meaningless
She can stop contraception immediately
She must continue contraception until age 55 regardless
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: She can stop contraception 1 year after this FSH result
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: In someone aged 50 or over who is amenorrhoeic on a non-injectable progestogen-only method, a one-off FSH of 30 IU/L or above allows contraception to stop 1 year later. This differs from CHC, which suppresses FSH and would need stopping for 6 weeks before testing; FSH is also unreliable on the injectable. The POP itself does not invalidate FSH interpretation.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 49-year-old woman controls her menopausal symptoms with combined (oestrogen + progestogen) HRT. She is sexually active and asks whether she still needs contraception. What is the most accurate statement?
options: HRT is not contraception — she still needs a contraceptive method until the appropriate stopping point
HRT prevents ovulation so no further contraception is needed
Combined HRT can simply be relied on for contraception once she reaches 50
She is too old to conceive so contraception is unnecessary
Contraception can stop now as she is on HRT
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: HRT is not contraception — she still needs a contraceptive method until the appropriate stopping point
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: HRT does not reliably suppress ovulation and is NOT contraceptive. A perimenopausal woman on HRT still needs contraception (until 55, or per the stopping criteria). A neat solution is an LNG-IUS providing both the HRT progestogen and contraception. A combined pill can be used to age 50 in a low-risk person as an alternative to HRT that also provides contraception, but HRT itself never becomes contraceptive at any age.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A woman who is 10 days postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding asks about contraception. She has no VTE risk factors. Which statement is correct?
options: Contraception is not needed until day 21, and CHC is UKMEC 4 for her because she is breastfeeding
She can start the combined pill now as she is breastfeeding
The lactational amenorrhoea method is unreliable this early
An IUD should be fitted today for best efficacy
She needs contraception immediately from day 1
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Contraception is not needed until day 21, and CHC is UKMEC 4 for her because she is breastfeeding
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Contraception is needed from day 21 postpartum (the ovulation risk before then is negligible). Because she is breastfeeding and under 6 weeks postpartum, CHC is UKMEC 4 and is deferred to 6 weeks — it would be UKMEC 3 in the first 21 days in someone not breastfeeding with no other VTE risk factors. LAM is in fact most effective early (fully breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + under 6 months). IUD timing is within 48 hours or from 4 weeks, not day 10.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A woman is 5 weeks postpartum, bottle-feeding, with no VTE risk factors, and wants to start the combined oral contraceptive pill. What is the correct advice regarding timing and extra precautions?
options: She can start now (UKMEC 2 from day 21 if not breastfeeding); use 7 days extra precautions
She can start now with no need for additional precautions
She must wait until 6 weeks as CHC is only safe then
CHC is contraindicated until 6 months postpartum
CHC is UKMEC 4 for her because she is postpartum
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: She can start now (UKMEC 2 from day 21 if not breastfeeding); use 7 days extra precautions
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: In a non-breastfeeding woman with no VTE risk factors, CHC is UKMEC 2 from day 21. At 5 weeks she can start now, and because it is after day 21 she needs 7 days of additional precautions. (The 6-week rule applies to breastfeeding women.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A breastfeeding woman is 3 weeks postpartum and wants the most convenient reliable long-term method she can start today. Which is appropriate?
options: Combined transdermal patch
Progestogen-only implant (UKMEC 1, safe in breastfeeding)
Immediate IUS insertion today
Wait until 6 months and use LAM until then
Combined oral contraceptive pill
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Progestogen-only implant (UKMEC 1, safe in breastfeeding)
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA) are UKMEC 1 from birth and safe in breastfeeding, so the implant can be inserted now. Combined methods are avoided (UKMEC 4 <6 weeks breastfeeding). IUD/IUS insertion is avoided in the 48h–4 week window (UKMEC 3). LAM alone would not be her long-term choice.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A woman requests an intrauterine device after her vaginal delivery. She is now 12 days postpartum. What is the correct advice about insertion timing?
options: Avoid insertion now — 48 hours to 4 weeks is UKMEC 3; insert at 4 weeks or later
Insert now, as long as she is not breastfeeding at all
Intrauterine devices are contraindicated for 6 months after any delivery
Insert now — any time postpartum is perfectly fine
Insert now but remove within 48 hours if symptomatic
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Avoid insertion now — 48 hours to 4 weeks is UKMEC 3; insert at 4 weeks or later
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: IUD/IUS should be inserted within 48 hours of delivery OR from ≥4 weeks. The 48h–4 week window is UKMEC 3 because of increased expulsion and roughly 6-fold perforation risk (recent delivery + breastfeeding). At day 12 she should wait until ≥4 weeks.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A woman relies on the lactational amenorrhoea method. Which single change means she can no longer rely on it for ~98% efficacy?
options: She had a normal vaginal delivery
She is exclusively breastfeeding on demand overnight
She has begun expressing and giving bottles of her own milk overnight
Her baby has just turned 3 months old
She has started giving some formula top-up feeds
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: She has started giving some formula top-up feeds
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: LAM is ~98% effective ONLY if all three hold: fully/exclusively breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + under 6 months postpartum. Introducing supplementary (formula) feeds breaks the 'fully breastfeeding' criterion, so efficacy falls and another method is needed. Being 3–4 months and still fully breastfeeding/amenorrhoeic is fine.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A trans man (assigned female at birth, retained uterus and ovaries) on testosterone therapy has amenorrhoea and is sexually active with a male partner. He asks whether he needs contraception. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Only condoms for STI protection are needed, not contraception
He still needs contraception — testosterone does not prevent pregnancy and is teratogenic
He should stop testosterone and use the combined pill instead
He does not need contraception as long as testosterone is continued
Testosterone-induced amenorrhoea means he cannot become pregnant
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: He still needs contraception — testosterone does not prevent pregnancy and is teratogenic
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Gender-affirming testosterone is NOT contraception: it often causes amenorrhoea but does not reliably prevent ovulation/pregnancy, and it is teratogenic (virilises an XX fetus). With a uterus/ovaries and pregnancy-risk sex he needs effective contraception, continued alongside (not instead of) testosterone.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: Which contraceptive methods are most appropriate for a person assigned female at birth taking testosterone who wants reliable contraception without opposing masculinisation?
options: Cyclical combined HRT
Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, IUS) or the copper IUD
Combined patch or vaginal ring
Combined oral contraceptive pill
High-dose oestrogen therapy
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, IUS) or the copper IUD
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Oestrogen-free methods are preferred because oestrogen opposes masculinisation (and carries a theoretical VTE concern): progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, IUS) and the copper IUD are ideal. Progestogens can additionally aid menstrual suppression/dysphoria. Testosterone is continued alongside.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A trans woman (assigned male at birth) on oestradiol and an anti-androgen has vaginal sex with a partner who has a uterus and ovaries. She has not had a vasectomy or orchidectomy. What is the correct advice about preventing pregnancy?
options: Fertile sperm may persist despite oestradiol — contraception is still needed
Only her partner's cervical screening needs arranging
She should stop oestradiol in order to reduce the pregnancy risk
Feminising hormones make her infertile, so no contraception is needed
A GnRH analogue can be added as reliable contraception
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Fertile sperm may persist despite oestradiol — contraception is still needed
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Oestradiol impairs but does not reliably abolish spermatogenesis, and GnRH analogues cannot be relied on for contraception. If fertile sperm may persist (no vasectomy/orchidectomy) and pregnancy is possible for the partner, contraception (barrier/partner method) is still required. Gender-affirming therapy is not stopped for this.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A healthy 41-year-old smoker (15/day) with no other risk factors requests the combined pill for cycle control. What is the correct advice?
options: Age 41 alone makes CHC UKMEC 2, so it is fine to start it
The progestogen-only injectable is contraindicated so offer CHC
CHC is entirely safe here, as she has no other risk factors
She must stop all contraception until she quits smoking
At 15 a day, aged 41, CHC is UKMEC 4 — recommend a non-oestrogen method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: At 15 a day, aged 41, CHC is UKMEC 4 — recommend a non-oestrogen method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: Smoking at age 35 or over raises CHC to UKMEC 3 (fewer than 15/day) or 4 (15 or more/day) because of cardiovascular and VTE risk. At 15 a day she falls in the 15-or-more group, so CHC is UKMEC 4 for her — an unacceptable risk, not a judgement call. A progestogen-only method (POP, implant, IUS) or a copper IUD is safer, and the LNG-IUS can also help cycle and bleeding control.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 45-year-old woman wants an IUS she can keep as long as possible for contraception. She is fitted with a 52 mg LNG-IUS today. Until what age can it be relied on for contraception, and what is the caveat if used for HRT?
options: Until 55 only if she is also on the combined pill
Only 5 years then it must be removed regardless
Until the menopause with no need to change it
Until 55; but change every 5 years if used as the HRT progestogen
Until 50; change every 3 years if used for HRT
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Until 55; but change every 5 years if used as the HRT progestogen
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: A 52 mg LNG-IUS inserted at ≥45 can be relied on for contraception until age 55. However, if it is also being used as the progestogen component of HRT it must be replaced every 5 years for endometrial protection.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A woman had a surgical abortion 3 days ago and wants to start contraception. What is the correct advice about timing?
options: She must wait for her next period before starting any method
Contraception is needed from day 5; most methods can be started immediately
Contraception is not needed for 3 weeks, as after childbirth
Contraception is needed from day 21, as postpartum
Only barrier methods can be used in the first month
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Contraception is needed from day 5; most methods can be started immediately
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: After miscarriage, abortion or ectopic, fertility can return quickly — ovulation can occur from about day 8 — so contraception is needed from day 5. Most methods can be started immediately, including at the time of the procedure. Starting today (day 3) she needs no additional precautions; had she presented on day 5 or later she would.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 50-year-old woman on the combined pill asks for an FSH test to see if she has reached the menopause so she can stop contraception. What is the correct advice?
options: FSH cannot be interpreted on CHC — switch off oestrogen first, or use age-based rules
A single low FSH result confirms the menopause even on the pill
Continue the combined pill until she reaches the age of 60
Check FSH now; if raised she can stop the pill immediately
FSH is never useful in deciding when to stop contraception
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: FSH cannot be interpreted on CHC — switch off oestrogen first, or use age-based rules
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: CHC suppresses FSH, so the result cannot be interpreted while on it (it would need stopping for ~6 weeks). The practical approach is to stop CHC at 50 and switch to a progestogen-only/non-hormonal method, then apply age/amenorrhoea rules (or the FSH option on a progestogen-only method).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.question: A 42-year-old woman has used the progestogen-only injectable for 6 years for contraception. What is the most appropriate management consideration relating to her age?
options: Switch her automatically to the combined pill instead
Double the dose to maintain efficacy in women over 40
Continue indefinitely, with no review needed at any point
Stop immediately as DMPA is contraindicated over 40
Review regularly for bone and cardiovascular risk; switch around age 50
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.answer: Review regularly for bone and cardiovascular risk; switch around age 50
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.explanation: The injectable over 40 warrants regular review because of concerns over bone mineral density loss and cardiovascular risk; it becomes UKMEC 2 over 45, all users should be reviewed at least 2-yearly, and at age 50 she should be counselled on risks and benefits and switched to an alternative. It is not absolutely contraindicated, but ongoing use should be an active, reviewed decision.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: How often is the progestogen-only injectable (DMPA) given, and by what route?
options: Daily orally
Monthly by IV
Weekly as a patch
Every 13 weeks by deep IM injection
Every 3 years subdermally
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Every 13 weeks by deep IM injection
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Intramuscular DMPA 150 mg is given by deep IM injection every 13 weeks; a subcutaneous 104 mg preparation can be self-administered after training.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: What is the primary mechanism of action of the contraceptive injection?
options: Only thickening cervical mucus
Copper toxicity to sperm
Preventing implantation as the main action
Only thinning the endometrium
Inhibition of ovulation (reliably, unlike the traditional POP)
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Inhibition of ovulation (reliably, unlike the traditional POP)
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: The injection reliably inhibits ovulation (its primary MOA), with mucus thickening and endometrial thinning secondary.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: Which side effect is most characteristically associated with the contraceptive injection?
options: Weight loss
Weight gain
Hypertension
Hair loss
Increased libido
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Weight gain
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: Weight gain (~2–3 kg over the first year) is the classic side effect most clearly associated with the injection.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: What is a distinctive drawback of the contraceptive injection compared with other progestogen methods?
options: Reduced bone mineral density
Increased bone density
Immediate reversibility
Daily dosing
STI protection
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Reduced bone mineral density
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.explanation: DMPA reduces bone mineral density (largely reversible after stopping), a distinctive drawback; it is also irreversible for ~3 months and delays fertility return.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.question: How long can the return of fertility be delayed after stopping the injection?
options: Permanently
Immediately
1 week
Up to about 12 months
1 month
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.answer: Up to about 12 months
